topic: The 1928 Disappearance of Glen and Bessie Hyde
title: The Dry Diary Found in an Empty 1928 River Boat
description:
In December 1928, searchers in the Lower Gorge of the Grand Canyon boarded the abandoned wooden sweep scow of newlyweds Glen and Bessie Hyde. Floating upright near River Mile 237, the boat still held their winter coats, food tins, Kodak camera, and Bessie Hyde's leather diary wrapped neatly in oilcloth.

In this documentary, we examine the exact mile-by-mile entries in Bessie's recovered diary, the developed photographs from her final roll of film, and Emery Kolb's Christmas Day search records to investigate how the physical state of the boat contradicts every simple explanation of their disappearance on the Colorado River.
thumbnail_prompt: Cinematic vintage 1920s photograph style, a wooden flat-bottomed river scow floating upright in a calm emerald canyon eddy surrounded by towering red and black Grand Canyon walls, hands in 1920s wool sleeves holding an oilcloth parcel over the wooden gunwale, dramatic morning canyon shadows, realistic textures, no text, no faces.

scenes.narration: A leather diary wrapped in oilcloth survived six miles of unmanned whitewater.
scenes.query: Glen and Bessie Hyde scow Grand Canyon 1928

scenes.narration: Searchers found it completely dry inside an empty wooden scow, right after its final entry logged passing River Mile 231 in the Grand Canyon.
scenes.query: Bessie Hyde diary Northern Arizona University

scenes.narration: How did the writer stow her journal in calm water, only for both passengers to vanish while their flat-bottomed boat stayed upright and dry?
Along the wooden gunwale of that abandoned twenty-foot boat, someone had carved forty-two small notches.
scenes.query: Close-up of a weathered rough-hewn wooden boat gunwale floating on silty river water in the 1920s, deep canyon shadow, no text or letters, cinematic documentary lighting

scenes.narration: Those forty-two marks matched the exact number of days between the boat's launch on October 20, 1928, and the final entry in Bessie Hyde's leather-bound diary on November 30.
scenes.query: Glen and Bessie Hyde sweep scow

scenes.narration: That alignment rules out the idea that the couple drifted helplessly inside the boat for days after November 30 without writing.
Whatever separated twenty-nine-year-old Glen Hyde and his twenty-two-year-old bride, Bessie, from their vessel happened on the forty-second day of their voyage.
scenes.query: Glen and Bessie Hyde portrait Emery Kolb 1928

scenes.narration: Yet the boat itself was not found near Mile 231, where Bessie recorded her last line.
scenes.query: Colorado River Grand Canyon map USGS

scenes.narration: On December 19, 1928, an Army search plane piloted by Lieutenant Muir S. Fairchild flew deep over the Lower Gorge of the Grand Canyon, within the Hualapai Indian Reservation.
scenes.query: Muir S. Fairchild U.S. Army Air Corps

scenes.narration: Looking down into a calm pool between River Mile 235 and River Mile 237, Fairchild spotted the twenty-foot-by-six-foot wooden sweep scow floating upright and intact.
scenes.query: 1920s biplane shadow passing over a narrow red rock canyon gorge with a tiny wooden flat-bottomed boat floating in a calm green eddy below, distant wide shot, no faces

scenes.narration: It took six more days for a ground and river team to reach it.
Glen's father, Idaho businessman Rollin C. Hyde, joined Grand Canyon Chief Ranger James P. Brooks and pioneering canyon photographers Emery and Ellsworth Kolb.
scenes.query: Emery and Ellsworth Kolb Grand Canyon

scenes.narration: Starting on December 21, the four men traveled to Peach Springs, Arizona, and hiked twenty-two miles down Peach Springs Wash to the mouth of Diamond Creek at River Mile 225.
There they spent three days patching an old, abandoned boat they found on the beach, launching into the frigid December current on the morning of Christmas Eve.
scenes.query: Four men in 1920s wool coats and trousers seen from behind repairing a weathered wooden rowboat on a sandy canyon beach beside a muddy river, overcast winter lighting

scenes.narration: When they finally pulled alongside the Hydes' scow on Christmas morning, December 25, 1928, the physical scene defied every expectation of a violent whitewater wreck.
scenes.query: Emery Kolb Glen Hyde scow recovery 1928

scenes.narration: The flat-bottomed craft was not smashed or overturned; it sat peacefully in an eddy because its long bow tow-line had snagged on submerged rocks, anchoring it against the current.
scenes.query: Heavy hemp rope stretching taut from the bow of an old wooden scow into dark silty river water, calm canyon reflection, 1920s documentary aesthetic

scenes.narration: About one foot of water sat in the bottom of the hull, yet every piece of cargo remained strapped down cleanly above the waterline.
Inside were food tins, camping gear, books, and even a metal bedspring frame that Glen had bolted onto the deck so the newlyweds could sleep comfortably.
scenes.query: Interior deck of a 1920s wooden river scow showing strapped canvas packs, tin cans, and an iron bedspring frame above shallow bilge water, no text, no people

scenes.narration: More troubling still, the search party found Glen's wallet with his cash, his firearm still resting in its holster, the couple's heavy winter coats, and Bessie's extra pair of shoes.
scenes.query: Vintage 1920s leather holster, folded wool coats, and women's leather lace-up shoes sitting neatly inside a wooden boat compartment, soft morning light

scenes.narration: Nobody hikes out of the Grand Canyon in late November without shoes, coats, money, food, or a weapon.
Yet when Emery Kolb developed the film from the Kodak camera found right beside Bessie's diary, the pictures revealed a second timeline contradiction starting sixty-six miles upstream.
Throughout the first five hundred miles of their journey down the Green and Colorado Rivers, the Hydes had used their Kodak camera constantly to document camps and rapids.
Bessie, a twenty-two-year-old amateur poet and artist born in Parkersburg, West Virginia, hoped their voyage would lead to book deals and paid lecture tours.
Her husband Glen, an experienced farmer and outdoorsman from Kimberly, near Twin Falls, Idaho, had an equally ambitious goal.
In 1926, Glen and his sister Jeanne had run Idaho's Salmon and Snake Rivers in a wooden sweep scow under the guidance of famed Idaho boatman Harry "Cap" Guleke.
For the Colorado River, Glen spent two days and fifty dollars in mid-October 1928 at Green River, Utah, building a twenty-foot-by-six-foot scow christened Rain-in-the-Face.
scenes.query: Man seen from behind in 1920s work clothes hammering thick wooden planks into a flat-bottomed river scow on a riverbank in Utah, autumn afternoon light, no text

scenes.narration: They aimed to set a speed record down the rivers and make Bessie the first documented woman to run the Grand Canyon.
In 1923, the United States Geological Survey had mapped the canyon, establishing Mile 0 at Lee's Ferry, Arizona, with mile numbers increasing downstream.
Bessie tracked those official USGS river miles carefully in her leather diary, while capturing the scenery on film.
When Emery Kolb developed the final roll recovered from the abandoned boat on Christmas Day, the last exposure showed Bessie standing in the scow below Tuckup Canyon, at River Mile 165.
scenes.query: Bessie Hyde in scow Mile 165 Grand Canyon

scenes.narration: Historians date that final photograph to approximately November 27, 1928.
Between Mile 165 on November 27 and Mile 231 on November 30, the couple navigated sixty-six miles of the Lower Gorge without taking a single picture on the remaining film.
scenes.query: Wooden sweep scow with two silhouettes standing at bow and stern entering a deep dark canyon gorge with towering black rock walls, late afternoon shadow, 1920s style

scenes.narration: That sixty-six-mile silence is especially puzzling because at Mile 179 sits Lava Falls, the most violent rapid in the entire Grand Canyon.
They survived Lava Falls, kept moving for fifty-two miles past it, and still never touched the shutter release.
Yet the lack of photographs did not mean they had stopped making camp or leaving physical traces along the riverbanks.
scenes.query: Sandy beach inside the Grand Canyon at dusk with a small dying campfire and a wooden scow pulled up against the shore, silhouettes in distance

scenes.narration: When the search party moved downstream from Diamond Creek at Mile 225, they discovered the couple's footprints pressed into the sandy beaches.
At the Diamond Creek camp from November 29, searchers found cold campfire ashes, empty tin cans, an empty jar of Idaho jam, and scattered lima beans.
scenes.query: Close-up of cold grey campfire ashes on a sandy riverbank surrounded by vintage 1920s tin cans, an empty glass jar without labels, and dried white beans, morning light

scenes.narration: Diamond Creek was the last accessible canyon exit point for dozens of miles.
If Bessie Hyde had been desperate to escape the river or her husband, Diamond Creek on November 29 was her moment to walk out.
To see whether she wanted to quit, we have to compare what witnesses said on the South Rim two weeks earlier against what Bessie actually wrote in her recovered diary.
On November 15, 1928, fifteen days before the diary stopped, the Hydes beached their scow at Bright Angel Creek, at River Mile 88 near Phantom Ranch.
From the river bottom, they hiked roughly nine miles up the Bright Angel Trail to Grand Canyon Village on the South Rim to buy supplies.

On November 16, they visited the cliffside studio of forty-seven-year-old Emery Kolb, who had famously filmed his own 1911 and 1912 voyage down the Green and Colorado Rivers with his brother Ellsworth.
scenes.query: Kolb Studio Grand Canyon South Rim

scenes.narration: Emery Kolb took their studio portrait and noticed a glaring omission in Glen's equipment list: the couple carried no life preservers or cork jackets.

Kolb warned them to take life jackets, and according to some secondary accounts, Glen mentioned that both he and Bessie had already been knocked overboard earlier in the trip and had to scramble back onto the scow.
scenes.query: Interior of a 1920s wooden photography studio overlooking a canyon, an older man holding a canvas cork life jacket speaking to a young couple in silhouette, warm window light

scenes.narration: Other historians note only that Glen nearly fell out at Lee's Ferry, but on one point every source agrees: Glen refused the life jackets.

While on the South Rim, the couple gave an interview to a Denver Post reporter and mailed letters to Glen's family stating they would not write again until they reached Needles, California, between December 6 and December 9.
scenes.query: Close-up of a woman's hand in a 1920s sleeve sealing a plain paper envelope at a wooden desk, vintage inkwell beside her, no legible text

scenes.narration: Just before hiking back down into the canyon on November 17, Bessie admired a pair of dress shoes worn by Emery Kolb's daughter, Edith, and reportedly gave away some of her own nice clothes.
As Bessie turned toward the trail, she remarked aloud, "I wonder if I shall ever wear pretty shoes again?"
Hiking down the trail with them that day was Adolph Gilbert Sutro, the grandson of a former San Francisco mayor and millionaire, who asked to hitch a one-day ride in their scow.
On November 18, 1928, the Hydes and Sutro ran the seven miles of rapids from Bright Angel Creek at Mile 88 to Hermit Creek at River Mile 95.
scenes.query: Hermit Rapid Grand Canyon Colorado River

scenes.narration: Sutro snapped photographs of the couple on the water before disembarking at Hermit Camp, watching them push off into Hermit Rapid.
scenes.query: Man in 1920s khaki touring clothes standing on a rocky canyon shore holding a small camera, watching a wooden scow enter churning whitewater rapids in the distance

scenes.narration: Adolph Sutro was the last person ever confirmed to see Glen and Bessie Hyde alive.

After the couple vanished, both Emery Kolb and Adolph Sutro stated for the record that during that mid-November stop, Bessie had appeared exhausted, apprehensive, and ready to quit right then and there.

Yet here is the archive contradiction: Bessie's own letters home from the South Rim, her Denver Post interview, and her leather diary entries all the way to November 30 express no terror and no marital conflict.
Written in a sparse, matter-of-fact tone, her log simply recorded daily miles, weather, and camps, right up to the moment they cleared 231 Mile Rapid on November 30.

Note that while nearly all modern sources and National Park Service archives state the final entry is dated November 30, matching the forty-two notches on the boat, a few older accounts, including a 1969 Utah Historical Quarterly article, state it was dated December 1.
scenes.query: Close-up of a gloved hand wrapping a small leather book carefully inside waterproof oilcloth on the deck of a wooden boat, calm canyon water around, no text

scenes.narration: Either way, for Bessie to write that they had passed Mile 231, wrap the book in oilcloth, and tuck it neatly away, the scow had to be in calm water below Mile 231.
And less than a mile ahead of that calm water waited one of the most dangerous low-water traps in the entire Grand Canyon.
Right below where Bessie packed her diary away sits 232 Mile Rapid, specifically at River Mile 232.4, a drop now listed in Grand Canyon boating guides as Honeymoon Rapid or Killer Fang Falls.
Colorado River historians Otis R. "Dock" Marston, author of From Powell to Power, and Brad Dimock, author of Sunk Without a Sound, examined what happens at Mile 232.4 during late-autumn water flows.

At low late-November flows under eight thousand cubic feet per second, the main current of the Colorado sweeps directly into a jagged, picket-fence-like row of submerged granite and metamorphic rocks called The Fangs.
scenes.query: Jagged dark granite rocks jutting just below the surface of a fast-moving silty brown river in a steep gorge, white foam pouring over submerged stone teeth, dramatic daylight

scenes.narration: Marston documented that Mile 232 has snared or damaged more boats at low water than almost any other spot in the canyon.
To understand how a twenty-foot wooden sweep scow behaves in such a rapid, historian Brad Dimock and his wife, Jeri Ledbetter, built an exact replica of Glen's boat in 1996.
scenes.query: Two river runners seen from behind standing upright at the bow and stern of a flat-bottomed wooden sweep scow, holding massive sixteen-foot wooden sweep oars in canyon rapids

scenes.narration: Becoming only the second couple in history to run the Grand Canyon in a sweep scow, Dimock discovered a terrifying mechanical flaw in Glen's design.
A sweep scow is steered by standing upright at the bow and stern, holding massive sixteen-foot wooden sweep oars.

Dimock reported that when waves hit the flat bow or the hull strikes a rock, those heavy sweep handles whip across the deck like "psychotic helicopter blades," easily capable of knocking a standing steersman unconscious or catapulting both passengers overboard.
scenes.query: Close dramatic angle of a heavy wooden sweep oar handle jerking violently across the wet wooden deck of a flat-bottomed boat in foaming brown river water, no people visible

scenes.narration: In fact, when Dimock and Ledbetter reached the middle of 232 Mile Rapid during their 1996 test run, they pulled their replica boat out of the main current to avoid suffering the Hydes' fate.
Under the accidental ejection theory proposed by Marston and Dimock, the Hydes' scow struck a submerged rock at Mile 232.4 and stopped dead or lurched violently.
scenes.query: Wooden flat-bottomed scow lurching against a submerged dark rock in churning brown river rapids, water spraying over the flat bow, distant angle, no faces

scenes.narration: Knocked into the freezing water without life jackets—or with one spouse jumping in to save the other—both would have been pulled down rapidly.

In 1928, before the Glen Canyon Dam was built, the Colorado River was thick with heavy sediment that routinely dragged drowning victims to the bottom and buried them in sandbars, explaining why no bodies were ever found.
scenes.query: Colorado River before Glen Canyon Dam

scenes.narration: By cruel coincidence, among Bessie's preserved youth writings at Northern Arizona University is a childhood poem about a doll in a creek that reads, "When I put her on the creek, / She sunk without a sound."
Freed of the couple's weight, the buoyant wooden scow would have washed off the rock at Mile 232 and drifted roughly five miles downstream until its trailing bowline snagged near Mile 237.
scenes.query: Empty wooden sweep scow drifting unmanned down a calm canyon river corridor between towering rock walls, long rope trailing from the bow

scenes.narration: What I keep coming back to is the pristine state of that boat when the Kolb brothers boarded it on Christmas morning.

If the scow slammed into the granite fangs of Mile 232 hard enough to throw both experienced handlers overboard, it is remarkable that the wooden hull suffered no major structural damage and ran five more miles of rapids unmanned without flipping or soaking Bessie's diary.
That exact physical puzzle led Glen's father, Rollin Hyde, and later Emery Kolb himself, to fear a much slower and more agonizing second theory.
Rollin Hyde noticed that an undamaged, un-capsized boat with dry supplies looks far more like a vessel that simply floated away from a beach than one that crashed in a rapid.
scenes.query: Wooden sweep scow gently bobbing near a sandy canyon bank as its loose bow rope slips off a wet rock into the current, 1920s visual style, no people

scenes.narration: Under this second theory, Glen and Bessie pulled ashore somewhere between Mile 232 and Mile 237 to scout a rapid or rest, and failed to secure the bowline tightly enough.

If the scow drifted out into the current and snagged downstream in a pool they could not reach on foot, the couple would have been stranded on the riverbank without food, coats, extra shoes, or Glen's firearm.
scenes.query: Two tiny silhouettes standing at the bottom of an immense sheer rock canyon wall looking out at a river bend, cold winter shadow, wide cinematic shot

scenes.narration: Forced to attempt to scale the sheer walls of the Lower Gorge to reach the rim, they could have perished of exposure or a fall in a remote side canyon.
This possibility haunted Emery Kolb because of what the search party did on Christmas Day, December 25, 1928.
Because the Kolb brothers were professional cinematographers, they brought a 16mm movie camera and still cameras on the rescue mission, filming the eerie, abandoned scow floating near Mile 237.

Unable to tow the two-ton wooden craft back upstream, the searchers unpacked the Hydes' personal effects, diary, and camera, and then cut the snagged bowline, sending the Rain-in-the-Face adrift downriver forever.
scenes.query: Close-up of a man's hand in a 1920s coat using a knife to slice a thick wet hemp rope tied to a wooden boat bow, silty river water below

scenes.narration: Kolb was later heavily criticized for cutting the boat loose and publicly regretted the decision for the rest of his life, worrying that if the Hydes were still alive on a ledge, he had destroyed their shelter and supplies.
Yet the evidence on the ground weighs heavily against the stranded-hiker theory.

Rollin Hyde financed and organized massive aerial, rim, and river searches across December 1928 and January 1929, personally hiking into the canyon and hiring skilled Hualapai trackers to comb the Lower Gorge.

While those trackers easily found the Hydes' footprints and lima beans upstream near Mile 225, they found zero footprints on the steep canyon walls around Mile 237 or leading up any side canyon below Mile 232.
scenes.query: Two Native American trackers in late 1920s hats and coats walking carefully along a narrow sandy ledge beside the Colorado River, examining the ground, seen from behind

scenes.narration: Then, in 1930, two years after the disappearance, a search party looking for a different drowning victim in the Lower Gorge stumbled across a deserted prospectors' cabin near the river.
scenes.query: Weathered abandoned wooden prospectors cabin tucked beneath rocky canyon cliffs in the 1930s, dusty afternoon sunlight, no text visible

scenes.narration: Written on the wall inside the cabin was the inscription: "Glen and Bessie Hyde November 31st 1928."
Because the month of November only has thirty days—and Bessie's diary ended on November 30—investigators quickly concluded the cabin graffiti was a macabre hoax by an unidentified canyon drifter.
That fake inscription was only the beginning of fifty years of sensational claims, confessions, and skeleton discoveries that tried to turn the Hydes' vanishing into a murder.
Even before the search ended, newspapers noticed how fast Glen and Bessie's romance had moved.
The pair had met in February 1927 aboard a passenger steamship traveling between San Francisco and Los Angeles, while Bessie was still married to her first husband, Earl Helmick.
scenes.query: Silhouette of a young man and woman in 1920s travel attire standing at the wooden railing of a coastal passenger steamship at sunset, looking at the ocean

scenes.narration: Helmick contested the divorce, forcing Bessie to relocate to Elko, Nevada, to meet residency requirements, where her decree was finalized on April 11, 1928.
The very next day, April 12, 1928—though a few secondary sources cite April 10—county records confirm she married Glen in Twin Falls, Idaho.
When they vanished seven months after the wedding, sensationalist newspapers briefly floated theories that a vengeful Earl Helmick had ambushed them in the canyon.

Decades later, canyon folklore shifted suspicion onto Bessie herself, proposing that she snapped near Diamond Creek, murdered a domineering Glen, staged the diary to indicate they went further, and hiked out to start a new life.
scenes.query: Lone figure in 1920s clothing walking up a wide dry desert wash between rocky canyon hills at dawn, seen from a great distance, no face

scenes.narration: In 1971, on a commercial raft trip through the Grand Canyon, a sixty-something passenger named Elizabeth Arnold Cutler announced around a campfire that she was Bessie Hyde and had stabbed abusive Glen to death before hiking out to Peach Springs.
When tracked down by reporters and researchers, Cutler recanted.

Birth certificates proved Cutler was a retired psychology professor known for playing mind games, born in Ohio roughly forty miles from Bessie's West Virginia birthplace, a few years apart, and significantly taller than Bessie.
scenes.query: Archivist hands wearing white cotton gloves comparing two vintage archival folders on a wooden library table, warm lamp light, no legible text

scenes.narration: Five years later, after Emery Kolb died in December 1976, workers found a male skeleton with a bullet hole in the skull inside a boat shed on Kolb's South Rim property.
scenes.query: Kolb Studio South Rim Grand Canyon

scenes.narration: Rumors immediately swirled that Kolb or Bessie had murdered Glen and hidden him on the rim, until forensic anthropology and dental testing by the Coconino County Medical Examiner proved the remains belonged to a man no older than twenty-two who had committed suicide around 1933.
A final wave of speculation arrived in 1992 after the death of pioneering female Grand Canyon outfitter Georgie White Clark.

Friends clearing Clark's estate found a pistol in her lingerie drawer, a birth certificate showing her real first name was Bessie—Bessie DeRoss—and a copy of Glen and Bessie Hyde's 1928 marriage certificate.
scenes.query: Open wooden dresser drawer from the 1990s containing a small vintage pistol beside folded fabric and old folded paper envelopes, no legible text

scenes.narration: However, biographer Richard Westwood and historian Brad Dimock proved through photographs, dental and physical comparisons, and early census records that Bessie DeRoss, born in Chicago or Oklahoma and raised in Colorado, was a completely different woman who simply collected canyon memorabilia.

Today, Bessie's original leather diary, her poetry book Wandering Leaves, the developed Kodak photos, and Emery Kolb's 16mm recovery footage sit preserved in the Special Collections and Archives at Cline Library, Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff.
scenes.query: Cline Library Northern Arizona University Flagstaff

scenes.narration: Whether the scow's final resting eddy was at Mile 235 as Kolb's photo log notes, or Mile 237 as National Park Service reports state, every homicide rumor has collapsed under forensic and archival scrutiny.
If you ask me, the truth lies right where Bessie's diary ended and where Brad Dimock nearly lost control of his replica scow: at the submerged granite fangs of Mile 232.4.

A sudden lurch against a low-water rock and a violent whip of sixteen-foot wooden sweep oars would have thrown both newlyweds into the silt-heavy current in a split second, leaving their lightened, flat-bottomed boat to drift five miles downstream with their coats, their shoes, and a dry leather diary that stopped on the edge of the rapid.
scenes.query: Wide atmospheric shot of the Colorado River at dusk in the Lower Gorge of the Grand Canyon, calm dark water reflecting red canyon walls, empty and quiet

scenes.narration: The river took the only two people who knew what happened after Mile 231, leaving behind a neatly packed boat that looked as if they had simply stepped away for a moment.

If this case stays with you, there is another file where fifteen men aboard the Pan American flying boat Hawaii Clipper vanished over the Philippine Sea in 1938, just eleven minutes after their radio officer politely asked ground control to stand by for one minute due to rain static.

watch_next.summary:
On July 29, 1938, the Pan American Airways flying boat Hawaii Clipper sent a routine position report over the Philippine Sea, followed eleven minutes later by a polite request from Flight Radio Officer William McGarty to stand by one minute due to rain static. No further word was ever heard from Captain Leo Terletzky or the fourteen other men aboard.

In this documentary, we examine the surviving Panay radio logs, the chemical laboratory tests on the USAT Meigs oil slick, and the Civil Aeronautics Authority report into the disappearance of the Martin M-130 aircraft NC14714 between Guam and Man
